study_identification_part.si4_title: Developmental trajectories of neuroanatomical alterations associated with the 16p11.2 Copy Number Variations

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To characterize age-related effects of 16p11.2 copy number variants on brain structure across childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood using a large normative developmental dataset for accurate age adjustment and to determine when these alterations appear and whether they evolve with age.

rci1_dataset_name.answer: NIHPD (NIH MRI study of normal brain development)

rci1_dataset_name.supporting_text: As normative reference data for brain growth, we used the multi-site longitudinal data from Objective 1 (i.e. initial time-point for enrolment from 4.5 to 18.5 years) of the publicly available NIHPD project (Evans and Brain Development Cooperative, 2006).

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Denoising; N3 intensity inhomogeneity correction; intensity normalization by histogram matching to ICBM152; 9-parameter linear registration to ICBM152; BEaST brain extraction; ANIMAL nonlinear registration; TBM with 10 mm FWHM Gaussian smoothing; Jacobian determinant calculation

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: The preprocessing steps applied to the native T1w images were (1) denoising, (2) intensity inhomogeneity correction using the N3 algorithm (Sled et al., 1998), and (3) intensity normalization by histogram matching to the ICBM152 template (Fonov et al., 2011). A hierarchical 9-parameter linear registration based on an intensity cross-correlation similarity measure was performed between the T1w images and the ICBM152 template ... Brain extraction was achieved using the Brain Extraction based on nonlocal Segmentation Technique (BEaST) (Eskildsen et al., 2012) ... Subsequently, images were non-linearly registered using the Automated Nonlinear Image Matching and Anatomical Labelling (ANIMAL) algorithm (Collins et al., 1995) ... A 3D Gaussian filter with FWHM of 10 mm was applied to the resulting inverted deformation grids. The Jacobian determinant of the deformation field was computed for every voxel, log-transformed

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Normative model: Scanner fixed effect tested but excluded due to non-significance and higher BIC. Linear correction: After Z-scoring with NIHPD norms, 16p11.2 control data were adjusted using a linear model (age + intercept) to correct for protocol differences (1.5T vs 3T; single vs multi-echo). This correction was applied to CNV carriers as well. The intercepts/slopes for correction were: total brain -0.68/-0.04; gray matter -0.11/-0.1; white matter 0.42/0.05; lateral ventricle -0.32/-0.02. Previous multisite analysis (Martin-Brevet et al., 2018) showed CNV-associated regions were not attributable to multisite artifacts.
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: During model selection, a fixed effect for individual scanner was tested but found to be not significant and the model was associated with a higher Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). ... We estimated a linear model that included Age and Intercept (i.e. bias and slope) for the Z-scored segmented volumes and the voxel-wise log-transformed Jacobian determinants of the 16p11.2 control data. The parameters of this linear model were used to adjust the 16p11.2 control dataset in order to obtain a mean Z-score of 0 for all ages. ... The same adjustment was applied to the CNV carrier groups. ... The intercepts and the slopes were, respectively -0.68/-0.04 for the total brain volume; -0.11/-0.1 for the gray matter volume (GM); 0.42/0.05 for the white matter volume (WM) and -0.32/-0.02 for the lateral ventricle (LV). ... Extensive analyses on the potential effect of these scanning sites and protocols were performed in a previous study showing that none of the regions associated with the 16p11.2 deletion or duplication could be attributed to artefacts introduced by the multisite analyses (Martin-Brevet et al., 2018).

nm1_model_origin.detail: Pre-trained normative model developed by Aubert-Broche et al. (2013) using NIHPD longitudinal data from 339 children (179 females, 160 males) scanned at 2-3 time points (874 total scans). Model uses mixed-effects framework to estimate age- and sex-related growth trajectories. See Aubert-Broche et al. (2013) NeuroImage for full details.
nm1_model_origin.supporting_text: We (Aubert-Broche et al., 2013) have previously developed a longitudinal image processing pipeline and Z-scoring method to adjust for age- and sex effects on brain growth trajectories using the NIH MRI study of normal brain development (NIHPD) (Evans and Brain Development Cooperative, 2006). ... The normative model (Aubert-Broche et al., 2011) used data from 339 children (179 females and 160 males), scanned longitudinally at 2 or 3 time points, with approximately 24 months between scans and mean age at first scan of 11.0 years, for a total of 874 scans.

Age was not divided into bins, but was considered as a continuous variable and was centered at 13 years - the mean age of NIHPD cohort. Linear effect of sex was also included in the fixed terms ... clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear models with genetic status (DEL, DUP, CTRL) as covariate applied to age/sex-adjusted Z-scores. Interaction terms (age*sex, age*group) tested. Bonferroni correction for global volumes (8 comparisons). False Discovery Rate (FDR q<0.05) correction for voxel-wise analyses. Anatomical labeling using neuromorphometric atlas.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: 16p11.2 deletions and duplications show mirror-effect brain alterations (deletions increased, duplications decreased volumes) that are present at 4.5 years and remain stable without age-related changes through 23 years, highlighting early-onset neuroimaging endophenotypes that persist across development.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: 16p11.2 CNVs show inverse gene dosage effects on brain structure. Deletions show increased volumes (Z-scores): total brain +1.165 (p<0.0001), gray matter +0.414 (p=0.00433), white matter +0.693 (p<0.0001). Duplications show decreased volumes (Z-scores): total brain -1.17 (p=0.0001), gray matter -0.631 (p=0.00272), white matter -0.53 (p=0.0018), lateral ventricles increased +1.629 (p<0.0001). Regional voxel-based analysis (TBM) identified mirror effects (DEL>CTRL>DUP) in bilateral calcarine cortex, insula, left transverse temporal gyrus, planum temporale, parietal operculum, and frontal/occipital white matter. Deletion-specific increases found in cuneus, anterior cingulate, posterior orbital and inferior frontal gyri. Deletion-specific decreases in bilateral cerebellum, middle cingulate, pallidum, putamen, precentral/postcentral gyri, fusiform, middle/inferior temporal gyri, supplementary motor cortex, gyrus rectus, left accumbens and angular gyrus. Duplication-specific decrease in occipital fusiform gyrus. Representative regions show effect sizes of Z = ±0.7 to ±1.6 across the full age range (4.5-23 years). No significant age*group or age*sex interactions were detected for any global or voxel-level measure, indicating alterations are established by 4.5 years and remain stable thereafter. Findings replicate previous results from Martin-Brevet et al. (2018) showing insula affected in both CNVs (mirror fashion) and calcarine cortex, temporal and precentral gyri altered in deletions.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: This study demonstrates that neuroimaging alterations associated with genetically defined neurodevelopmental risk (16p11.2 CNVs) are present early and stable across development, contrasting with behavioral/symptom trajectories that evolve rapidly during the same period. The stability of the neuroimaging endophenotype from 4.5 to 23 years suggests brain alterations may precede or underlie symptom emergence and evolution. Results are consistent with findings in idiopathic ASD and other genetic syndromes (Fragile X, 22q11.2 deletion) showing early-established brain differences. Mouse models of 16p11.2 deletion show alterations in insula and striatum at postnatal day 7 (equivalent to prenatal period in humans), suggesting very early developmental onset. The normalization approach using large external normative datasets enables study across broad age ranges despite nonlinear brain growth. Data in neonates and toddlers will be needed to pinpoint exact onset timing of alterations.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Technical differences in acquisition (1.5T NIHPD vs 3T 16p11.2; multi-center variability) may affect registration quality. Future normative curves should incorporate additional variables (ancestry, field strength, demographics). Broad age range may introduce age-dependent motion artifacts, though thorough QC was performed and no age-related findings emerged. Limited power to detect small age-related changes (smallest detectable: DEL 0.07-0.12 Z-score/year; DUP 0.09-0.16 Z-score/year). Uncertainty for lower age range; larger sample of younger participants needed. Results may not generalize to CNV carriers with extreme obesity or severe ASD unable to complete scanning. Cohort representative of broader 16p11.2 IQ and psychiatric symptoms but sample size limits investigation of onset at very young ages.
